newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate starts debate on tax cut legislation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate starts debate on tax cut legislation.

text.p: The Senate on Wednesday began debating tax cut legislation on a bipartisan note, but ran into opposition from Democratic leaders.

Senate Democrats planned to offer an alternative five-year tax cut plan, despite the fact that Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee helped draft the bill under consideration and approved it last week.
The tax legislation aims to implement the requirement in the balanced-budget agreement of an $85 billion net tax cut over five years.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth opened the tax debate by stressing that the Senate bill had been drafted in a bipartisan manner.

But he acknowledged the opposition. "I realise that in the course of debating this proposal on the floor, there will be those who stand against this bipartisan bill," the Delaware Republican said. "In a partisan effort, there will be those who attack this tax relief bill."

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, the senior Democrat on the Finance Committee, said he had helped shape the bill. "The resulting legislation is not altogether what some of us would prefer, but even so it does include a number of redeeming provisions," he said in a statement.
The Senate tax bill, due to changes by the Finance Committee, amounted to a $77 billion net tax cut with another $8 billion slated for child health spending.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said changes were being discussed that would raise the tax cut to a net $85 billion over five years by providing tax relief for small businesses.
"We have some other small business provisions that we would like very much to have in our package, and we are looking at those," the Mississippi Republican said.

Senate Democrats said their plan would take into account not only income taxes but also payroll taxes when providing a child tax credit and that would extend the credit to seven million The Senate Democrat plan would exclude from taxation 30 percent of gains made on investments such as stocks for people of all income levels. The Republican plan would cut the maximum individual capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent.

The Democrat proposal would use identical tax and revenue increases set out in the Republican bill. Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said the new plan had "very broad" support among Senate Democrats.

Senators Wednesday offered amendments to allow victims of natural disasters to tap into Individual Retirement Accounts, to limit capital gains tax relief, to increase the cigarette tax, and to remove the depletion allowance for certain mining. Votes on amendments will start on Thursday.
The House is scheduled to debate and vote on its tax legislation on Thursday. Democrats and the White House have strongly objected to provisions in that bill.
"Democrats will oppose it because well over half the benefits go to the richest five percent of taxpayers," House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri said.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said Democratic calculations end up classifying middle-income families as rich and denying tax relief to them.
